(CNN) -- Madagascar's military handed over the reins of the island nation to opposition leader Andry Rajoelina on Wednesday, ending a two-month long political crisis -- but apparently creating a constitutional one. Andry Rajoelina is six years too young to be Madagascar's president under its constitution. Rajoelina, a former disc jockey turned mayor of Madagascar's capital, declared himself president of a transitional government and his supporters pledged to hold elections in two years. But Rajoelina, at 34, is six years too young to be president, according to the country's constitution. Also, the constitution says the head of parliament's upper house must call elections within two months if something happens to the president. Madagascar's former president, Marc Ravalomanana, ceded power to his military Tuesday after insisting over the weekend that he would remain in control. Analysts think Ravalomanana had little choice but to step down once he had lost much of the army's support. The African Union had warned that any power transfer aided by the military would amount to a coup d' etat. The Union has since removed any mention of a coup in its official communique and called on the transitional government to "comply scrupulously with the provisions of the constitution of Madagascar on interim arrangements." Monja Roindefo, the opposition-appointed prime minister, vigorously defended the week's developments on the island, located off the southeastern coast of Africa. "Well, we would like to define what is a coup," he told CNN on Wednesday. "A coup is a group of people or persons who takes the power on behalf of sovereignty, on behalf of the people ... when the representative democracy doesn't work anymore." "As you know, as stated, in the African Union charter, the people have the right to defend itself from an oppression or a dictatorship in Africa," he added. Roindefo said the new government will hold elections but has given itself two years to clean up the process.  Watch more from iReporters and Twitterers on the crisis » . "How could you make an election immediately?" he said. "We need to reform the electoral commission. ... So the 24 months that we have given ourselves is to prepare all these types of elections in order to build a genuine democratic country." The African Union also asked that all steps be taken to ensure the safety of the former president. The opposition leader had called for Ravalomanana's arrest, accusing him of corruption, financial mismanagement and dictatorship. Ravalomanana was first elected in 2001 and won a second term in 2006. To many Malagasy, he represented a new breed of politician -- a self-made millionaire, a no-nonsense business leader. But Ravalomanana maintained his business empire while in office and it was unclear to many where his business interests ended and his political leadership began. His recent purchase of a $60 million airplane further stoked public discontent. Opposition leader Rajoelina was quick to seize on the sentiments and made fiery appeals to the country's impoverished masses. The country was plunged into political instability in January after thousands of people took to the streets to protest rising food prices and what they perceived as autocratic behavior by Ravalomanana. The protests soon degenerated into rioting and looting, and left about 100 people dead.  Watch more on president's resignation » . Soon after, Rajoelina declared that he was in charge of the country. He gave Ravalomanana until early February to step down. The president responded by firing Rajoelina as mayor of the capital, inciting the latter's supporters to once again descend on the streets. More deadly violence followed. Clashes spread to most provincial capitals and other cities across the country, with homes and businesses looted and burned, the U.S. State Department reported. CNN's David McKenzie contributed to this report.

According to Madagascar's constitution, Andry Rajoelina falls short of the presidential age requirement by six years.

Rajoelina, who once worked as a disc jockey before becoming mayor of the nation's capital, proclaimed himself leader of a transitional administration, while his followers vowed that elections would take place within a two-year window. However, at age 34, Rajoelina does not meet the constitutional minimum age for the presidency, which he misses by six years. Furthermore, the constitution stipulates that if anything happens to the president, the leader of parliament's upper chamber is required to schedule elections within a two-month period.

The country's previous leader, Marc Ravalomanana, surrendered authority to the military on Tuesday, despite having declared over the weekend that he intended to keep his grip on power. Observers believe that once he had forfeited a significant portion of the army's backing, Ravalomanana had few alternatives beyond resignation.

The African Union had cautioned that any handover of power supported by the military would constitute a coup. Since then, the Union has stripped all references to a coup from its formal statement and urged the transitional leadership to "comply scrupulously with the provisions of the constitution of Madagascar on interim arrangements."

Monja Roindefo, whom the opposition installed as prime minister, strongly justified the events that had unfolded on the island, which sits off Africa's southeastern coastline. "Well, we would like to define what is a coup," he stated to CNN on Wednesday. "A coup is a group of people or persons who takes the power on behalf of sovereignty, on behalf of the people ... when the representative democracy doesn't work anymore."

He went on to say, "As you know, as stated, in the African Union charter, the people have the right to defend itself from an oppression or a dictatorship in Africa."

Roindefo indicated that although the incoming government intends to organize elections, it has allotted itself a two-year timeframe to reform the system. "How could you make an election immediately?" he questioned. "We need to reform the electoral commission. ... So the 24 months that we have given ourselves is to prepare all these types of elections in order to build a genuine democratic country."

The African Union additionally requested that every measure be taken to guarantee the former president's safety. The opposition leader had demanded that Ravalomanana be detained, leveling charges of corruption, financial misconduct, and dictatorial rule against him.

Ravalomanana initially came to power through election in 2001 and secured a second term in 2006. For numerous Malagasy citizens, he embodied a fresh kind of leader—a millionaire who had built his own fortune and a straightforward business executive. Yet he continued running his business empire during his time in office, and for many, the boundary between his commercial ventures and his role as a political leader remained blurry. Public frustration grew even further when he recently acquired a $60 million aircraft.

Opposition leader Rajoelina wasted no time capitalizing on this public mood, delivering passionate appeals to the nation's poverty-stricken population.

The nation descended into political turmoil in January when thousands filled the streets to demonstrate against climbing food costs and what they viewed as Ravalomanana's authoritarian conduct. The demonstrations quickly deteriorated into riots and looting, ultimately claiming roughly 100 lives.

Shortly afterward, Rajoelina announced that he had taken command of the country, giving Ravalomanana a deadline of early February to relinquish power. The president countered by dismissing Rajoelina from his position as mayor of the capital, which prompted Rajoelina's backers to flood the streets once more. Additional lethal violence ensued. According to the U.S. State Department, the confrontations extended to the majority of provincial capitals and other urban areas throughout the nation, with residences and businesses being plundered and set ablaze.

# Madagascar's Military Hands Power to Opposition Leader Amid Constitutional Crisis

**ANTANANARIVO, Madagascar** — Madagascar's political turmoil reached a dramatic climax this week as the military transferred power to opposition leader Andry Rajoelina, following the resignation of President Marc Ravalomanana under intense pressure from armed forces.

The transfer of authority marks the end of a months-long standoff that has left dozens dead and plunged the Indian Ocean island nation into its worst political crisis in years. However, the manner of the transition has raised serious constitutional questions and drawn international condemnation.

## A Contested Rise to Power

Rajoelina, the 34-year-old former mayor of the capital Antananarivo, has emerged as the central figure in the crisis. A former disc jockey turned politician, he had positioned himself as the leader of an opposition movement demanding Ravalomanana's removal, accusing the president of authoritarian rule and mismanagement.

Yet Rajoelina faces an immediate and significant obstacle: at 34, he falls short of the minimum age of 40 required by Madagascar's constitution to serve as president. This constitutional barrier casts a shadow over the legitimacy of the power transfer and complicates any path toward internationally recognized leadership.

## International Community Cries "Coup"

The African Union and numerous foreign governments have refused to recognize the transition, characterizing it as an unconstitutional seizure of power. The distinction matters enormously in a region where military-backed transfers of authority have historically triggered diplomatic isolation and economic consequences.

Critics argue that regardless of grievances against Ravalomanana's administration, replacing an elected leader through military intervention undermines democratic norms and sets a troubling precedent for the continent.

Supporters of Rajoelina counter that Ravalomanana had lost the mandate to govern and that the changes reflect the will of demonstrators who had filled the streets for weeks.

## The Fall of Ravalomanana

Ravalomanana, a wealthy businessman who built a dairy empire before entering politics, had governed since 2002. His presidency, initially marked by promises of development and reform, eventually became mired in allegations of concentrating power and enriching allies.

The final blow came as segments of the military withdrew their support, leaving the president with few options. His departure created the power vacuum that Rajoelina moved quickly to fill.

## Uncertain Path Forward

The constitutional questions surrounding Rajoelina's eligibility, combined with the international refusal to recognize the new arrangement, suggest that Madagascar's crisis may be far from over. Analysts warn that without a legitimate constitutional framework and broad recognition, the country risks prolonged instability, potential aid suspensions, and continued division.

The coming weeks will likely determine whether Rajoelina can consolidate his position or whether pressure from regional bodies and internal opposition forces a negotiated settlement or new elections.

For ordinary Malagasy citizens, already grappling with widespread poverty, the political uncertainty adds another layer of hardship to daily life in one of the world's poorest nations.

*This is a developing story.*

# Ravalomanana Steps Down Amid Political Crisis; Power Transferred to Rajoelina

## Political Turmoil Culminates in Presidential Resignation

Madagascar's political crisis reached a dramatic turning point in March 2009 when President Marc Ravalomanana stepped down from power, ceding authority amid weeks of escalating violence, protests, and mounting pressure from the military and opposition forces.

The resignation followed months of confrontation between Ravalomanana and Andry Rajoelina, the former mayor of the capital, Antananarivo. The standoff had paralyzed the island nation and left dozens dead in clashes between security forces and demonstrators.

## The Transfer of Power

Under intense pressure, Ravalomanana reportedly attempted to hand power to a military directorate. However, this arrangement quickly gave way as the military threw its support behind Rajoelina, who at 34 was below the constitutional minimum age of 40 for the presidency.

Rajoelina subsequently assumed leadership as head of a transitional authority, styling himself as president of a "High Transitional Authority." He pledged to organize new elections within a period of up to two years and to draft a new constitution.

Ravalomanana, a self-made businessman who had risen from selling homemade yogurt to building a dairy empire before entering politics, departed the country. He would spend subsequent years in exile, primarily in South Africa.

## African Union Condemnation

The African Union (AU) responded swiftly and sharply to the developments, characterizing the transfer of power as an unconstitutional seizure of authority.

Key elements of the AU's response included:

- **Suspension of Madagascar** from the organization, a move designed to signal that the change in leadership violated the bloc's principles governing democratic governance and constitutional order.
- **Condemnation of the takeover** as a coup d'état, with AU officials rejecting the legitimacy of the new administration.
- **Calls for a return to constitutional order** and demands that any political resolution respect democratic norms.

Then-AU Commission Chairman Jean Ping was among the officials who articulated the organization's position, emphasizing that the continental body would not endorse changes of government achieved through unconstitutional means.

## International Reaction

The African Union's stance was echoed by other international actors. The Southern African Development Community (SADC) also condemned the events and suspended Madagascar's membership. Various Western governments and international organizations expressed concern, with some suspending non-humanitarian aid to the impoverished nation.

## Background to the Crisis

The conflict between the two leaders had deep roots. Rajoelina had emerged as a fierce critic of Ravalomanana, accusing him of authoritarianism and mismanagement. Tensions had been inflamed by government actions including the closure of a television station owned by Rajoelina.

Disputes over land deals, economic policy, and governance further widened the rift, ultimately fueling the popular unrest and military intervention that brought down Ravalomanana's government.

## Aftermath

The change in leadership ushered in a prolonged period of political instability and international isolation for Madagascar. The transitional government struggled to gain international recognition, and the delayed promise of elections extended the country's diplomatic limbo for several years.

---

*This report reflects events surrounding Madagascar's 2009 political crisis. For the most current developments, readers should consult up-to-date news sources.*

# Madagascar in Turmoil: The 2009 Coup and Its Constitutional Contradictions

*A closer look at the political crisis that toppled a president and installed a leader too young to legally hold office*

---

Madagascar, the vast island nation off Africa's southeastern coast, descended into political chaos in early 2009 as a power struggle between President Marc Ravalomanana and opposition figure Andry Rajoelina culminated in what much of the international community condemned as a coup d'état. The crisis exposed deep economic grievances, urban discontent, and a striking constitutional paradox at its center.

## The Constitutional Age Problem

At the heart of the controversy sat an unavoidable legal contradiction: Andry Rajoelina, the former mayor of the capital Antananarivo who seized power in March 2009, was only 34 years old. Madagascar's constitution set the minimum age for the presidency at 40.

Rajoelina and his supporters worked around this obstacle by declaring him head of a transitional authority — the High Transitional Authority — rather than president in the constitutional sense. This maneuver allowed him to assume executive power while sidestepping, at least rhetorically, the age requirement that would have barred him from the office under normal electoral circumstances.

Critics seized on this contradiction as evidence that the transfer of power was fundamentally illegitimate. The African Union suspended Madagascar's membership, and the Southern African Development Community (SADC) refused to recognize the new government, citing both the unconstitutional nature of the takeover and the involvement of the military in forcing Ravalomanana from office.

## Background to the Unrest

The roots of the crisis stretched back months. Rajoelina, a charismatic former disc jockey and media entrepreneur, had built a political base as mayor of the capital. Tensions escalated sharply when the government shut down his television station, Viva, after it aired an interview with the exiled former president Didier Ratsiraka — a direct challenge to Ravalomanana's authority.

The closure ignited public anger that fed on pre-existing grievances. Many urban Malagasy resented what they saw as Ravalomanana's increasingly autocratic style and the blending of his personal business empire with the machinery of state. A particularly inflammatory issue was a reported deal to lease vast tracts of farmland to the South Korean company Daewoo — an arrangement widely perceived as selling off the nation's patrimony.

Demonstrations turned deadly. In early February 2009, security forces opened fire on protesters marching toward the presidential palace, killing dozens. The bloodshed hardened opposition resolve and eroded Ravalomanana's standing. As weeks passed, segments of the military began defecting to Rajoelina's side, and by mid-March the president's position had become untenable. Ravalomanana ultimately handed power to a military directorate, which promptly transferred authority to Rajoelina.

## Voices from the Opposition

*[Editorial note: The quotations below are presented as illustrative of the kinds of statements made by figures in Ravalomanana's camp during this period. For a publishable piece, these should be verified against primary sources and press archives, and attributed to specific named individuals and dates.]*

Ravalomanana's appointed prime minister and loyalists denounced the takeover in the strongest terms, framing it as a naked seizure of power by force.

> "What has happened here is not a revolution of the people — it is a coup carried out at gunpoint. No amount of ceremony can make an illegal act legal."

They pressed the international community to withhold recognition and pointed directly to the constitutional issue:

> "The constitution is clear. A man who cannot legally stand for the presidency cannot simply invent a new title and claim the same powers. This is a mockery of our laws."

Officials also warned of the precedent being set:

> "If we allow the streets and the barracks to decide who governs Madagascar, we abandon the ballot box altogether. That is a dangerous road for every young democracy in Africa."

## Aftermath and International Response

The international reaction was swift and largely unified in its condemnation. Beyond the AU and SADC suspensions, donor nations froze significant portions of non-humanitarian aid — a heavy blow to one of the world's poorest countries, heavily dependent on external assistance.

Rajoelina pledged to hold fresh elections and guide the country through a transitional period, but the crisis left Madagascar politically isolated and economically strained for years. Negotiations mediated by regional bodies repeatedly stalled, and a durable resolution to restore constitutional order proved elusive well beyond 2009.

The events of that year remain a case study in the fragility of institutions when economic frustration, personal rivalry, and military intervention converge — and in how a legal technicality over something as simple as a candidate's age can become emblematic of a much larger question of legitimacy.

## Overview

Madagascar, the vast island nation off the southeastern coast of Africa, has endured a period of profound political instability marked by popular protests, a military intervention, and contested claims of governmental legitimacy. What began as demonstrations over basic living conditions escalated into a full-blown constitutional crisis, testing the resilience of the country's democratic institutions and raising serious questions about the direction of one of the world's poorest nations.

## The Roots of Discontent

Madagascar's political turmoil did not emerge in a vacuum. The country has long struggled with chronic poverty, with a significant portion of its roughly 30 million people living below the international poverty line. Persistent challenges have included:

- **Economic hardship**: Rising costs for staple foods, fuel, and basic necessities placed enormous strain on ordinary citizens.
- **Infrastructure deficiencies**: Frequent power outages and water shortages fueled public frustration, particularly in urban centers.
- **Governance concerns**: Allegations of corruption and questions about the concentration of power contributed to eroding trust in state institutions.

These structural problems created fertile ground for popular unrest when triggered by immediate grievances.

## Food Price Protests and Escalating Unrest

The immediate spark for the crisis came from demonstrations centered on the soaring cost of living. As prices for essential goods climbed and public services deteriorated, citizens—many of them young people facing bleak economic prospects—took to the streets to voice their anger.

What started as protests over food prices, utilities, and economic desperation rapidly broadened in scope. Demonstrators increasingly directed their frustrations toward the government itself, transforming economic grievances into political demands. The protests reflected a deep-seated sense that leadership had failed to address the basic needs of the population.

## Violence and Loss of Life

As the demonstrations intensified, so too did the violence. Confrontations between protesters and security forces, along with associated rioting and looting, resulted in a significant death toll. Reports indicated that approximately 100 people died during the unrest, though figures were disputed and difficult to verify independently amid the chaos.

The loss of life marked a grim turning point, hardening positions on all sides and deepening the sense of national crisis. The scale of the casualties drew international attention and condemnation, with human rights organizations calling for restraint and accountability.

## The Military's Decisive Role

The pivotal moment in the crisis came with the involvement of the military. As pressure mounted, elements of Madagascar's armed forces—reportedly including elite units—played a decisive role in shifting the balance of power. Rather than continuing to suppress the demonstrations, key military factions aligned themselves with the protest movement or otherwise withdrew support from the existing government.

This military intervention proved instrumental in the collapse of the sitting administration and the subsequent establishment of a new transitional authority. The role of the armed forces echoed Madagascar's history, as the country has experienced previous episodes in which the military served as a kingmaker during periods of political upheaval.

The involvement of soldiers in effecting a change of government carried significant implications. While some celebrated the military's actions as a response to popular will, others expressed deep concern about the precedent of armed forces determining the nation's political leadership outside constitutional processes.

## A Contested Transition

The formation of a new transitional government did not resolve the crisis so much as usher in a new phase of it. The legitimacy of the new authorities became a central point of contention, both domestically and internationally.

### Domestic Divisions

Within Madagascar, opinions on the transitional government were sharply divided. Supporters viewed the change as a necessary correction that reflected the demands of a population pushed to its limit. Critics, however, questioned whether power had been seized through unconstitutional means, raising fears about the erosion of democratic norms.

### International Response

The international community reacted with caution and, in many quarters, concern. Regional and global bodies have historically taken a firm stance against unconstitutional changes of government. Key considerations included:

- **The African Union**: The AU has a well-established policy against coups and irregular transfers of power, often suspending member states that experience such changes. Madagascar faced the prospect of diplomatic isolation and potential suspension.
- **Regional organizations**: Southern African bodies expressed concern about stability and the implications for the broader region.
- **International partners**: Foreign governments and institutions weighed how to respond, balancing concerns about democratic principles against the practical realities on the ground.

The disputed legitimacy of the new government threatened to complicate Madagascar's access to international assistance and its standing in the community of nations—matters of considerable importance for a country heavily dependent on external support.

## Historical Context

Madagascar's recent crisis must be understood against the backdrop of its turbulent political history. The nation has weathered multiple episodes of instability since gaining independence from France in 1960. Notably, previous transfers of power have been marred by controversy, disputed elections, and extra-constitutional maneuvering.

This pattern of recurring instability has hampered the country's development and undermined efforts to build durable democratic institutions. Each crisis has left lasting scars, contributing to a cycle in which economic hardship fuels political unrest, which in turn deepens economic distress.

## Challenges Ahead

The path forward for Madagascar remains fraught with uncertainty. Several critical challenges confront the nation:

1. **Restoring legitimacy**: Any transitional authority must establish credibility both at home and abroad, likely requiring a credible roadmap toward elections and constitutional governance.

2. **Addressing root causes**: The economic grievances that ignited the protests—poverty, high food prices, and inadequate services—demand substantive solutions, not merely political change.

3. **National reconciliation**: Healing the divisions exposed by the crisis, including addressing the deaths that occurred, will be essential for long-term stability.

4. **International reintegration**: Reassuring international partners and avoiding isolation will be crucial for a nation that relies on foreign aid and investment.

5. **Preventing recurrence**: Breaking the cycle of instability requires building institutions robust enough to withstand future pressures.

## Conclusion

Madagascar's two-month political crisis represents a significant moment in the nation's history, encapsulating the interplay of economic desperation, popular mobilization, military intervention, and contested authority. The demonstrations that began over the price of food and the reliability of basic services ultimately reshaped the country's political landscape, at the cost of roughly 100 lives.

As the new transitional government seeks to consolidate its position amid questions about its legitimacy, the fundamental challenges that drove citizens into the streets remain unresolved. Whether Madagascar can translate this moment of upheaval into meaningful and lasting change—or whether it will follow the well-worn path of recurring instability—remains one of the central questions facing the island nation and those who watch its fate with concern.

# Rajoelina Declares Himself President of Madagascar Amid Political Turmoil

**ANTANANARIVO, Madagascar** — In a dramatic escalation of the island nation's political crisis, opposition leader Andry Rajoelina declared himself president of Madagascar, seizing power from the country's elected leadership and plunging the Indian Ocean nation into constitutional uncertainty.

## A Contested Power Grab

Rajoelina, the former mayor of Antananarivo, announced that he was assuming control of the country and its transitional government. The declaration came after weeks of mounting opposition protests, deadly clashes between demonstrators and security forces, and growing pressure on the sitting government.

The move immediately raised questions about its legitimacy, with critics and international observers characterizing it as an unconstitutional seizure of power backed by defecting elements of the military.

## Is It a Coup?

The central question surrounding Rajoelina's declaration is whether it constitutes a coup d'état. Several factors point toward that characterization: the transfer of power occurred outside constitutional processes, key military units switched allegiance to Rajoelina, and the transition bypassed established democratic mechanisms.

International bodies and legal experts noted that when a leader assumes power through military backing rather than through elections or constitutional succession, it typically meets the definition of a coup — regardless of the popular grievances that may have preceded it.

## The African Union's Response

The African Union took a firm stance against the power transfer, consistent with its longstanding policy of rejecting unconstitutional changes of government. The AU has historically suspended member states that experience coups, and it moved to condemn the events in Madagascar as a violation of its principles.

The continental body called for a return to constitutional order and warned against any government that came to power through illegitimate means. Regional organizations, including the Southern African Development Community (SADC), echoed concerns about the breakdown of democratic norms.

## A History of Bitter Rivalry

The crisis is deeply rooted in the personal and political feud between Rajoelina and Marc Ravalomanana, a rivalry that has defined Madagascar's turbulent politics.

Ravalomanana, a wealthy businessman who built a dairy empire, rose to the presidency and governed the nation before the two men became bitter adversaries. Their conflict pitted Ravalomanana's establishment power against Rajoelina's populist appeal as a young, charismatic mayor who positioned himself as a champion of ordinary Malagasy citizens.

Tensions between the two escalated over accusations of authoritarianism, economic mismanagement, and heavy-handed responses to public dissent. The rivalry has repeatedly destabilized the country, contributing to cycles of protest, contested elections, and challenges to governmental authority.

## An Uncertain Future

As Rajoelina consolidates his claim to power, Madagascar faces an uncertain path forward. The international community's refusal to recognize governments that seize power unconstitutionally could lead to diplomatic isolation and suspended aid, deepening the economic hardship in one of the world's poorest nations.

The situation remains fluid, with the potential for further unrest as competing factions vie for control and the population braces for the consequences of yet another rupture in the nation's fragile democratic order.
